explain.say: Train wheels have no steering, yet they stay on narrow rails at high speed. Many people think the flanges, the lips on the inside edge, do the job, but the real secret is the shape of the wheel.

faq.a: A cone-shaped tread means each wheel rolls on a bigger or smaller circle depending on where it touches the rail. That lets the wheelset steer itself back to the centre.

faq.q: Why are both wheels fixed to one axle?
faq.a: Fixing both wheels to a solid axle makes them turn together. Combined with the cones, any difference in the circles they roll on steers the wheelset.
asks: Do train wheels have a differential?

faq.q: How do train wheels go round corners?
faq.a: On a curve the wheelset shifts outward, so the outer wheel rolls on its larger part and covers the longer outside path while the inner wheel rolls on its smaller part. No differential is needed.
asks: How do trains turn without steering?

faq.a: The flange is a raised lip on the inside edge of a train wheel. It stops the wheel slipping off on very sharp curves and guides it through points, but in normal running it rarely touches the rail.
asks: Do flanges keep trains on the track?

faq.q: Why do trains screech on tight bends?
faq.a: On tight curves the cones cannot fully make up the difference in path length, so the wheels slip and the flanges rub against the rail, making a squeal.

facts: Train wheel treads are slightly cone-shaped, so a wheelset centres itself on the track.
The two wheels on a train axle are fixed together and turn at the same speed.
The gentle side-to-side swaying of a self-centring wheelset is called hunting oscillation.
